title.rendered: From Northfield to the North Central Council of Latin Americanists

content.rendered:
In this Faculty View reflection, Associate Professor of Romance Languages and Patricia Boldt Distinguished Teaching Professor in the Humanities Kristina Medina-Viariño shares how community-engaged scholarship connects St. Olaf College students with wider scholarly conversations.

When St. Olaf College student Zareth Pérez ’28 presented “Mi Gente de Northfield: An Oral History Project on Latinidad in Southern Minnesota” at the North Central Council of Latin Americanists (NCCLA) conference at Viterbo University, she brought oral history research rooted in Northfield into a regional scholarly conversation. 

Pérez was the only St. Olaf student presenting, joining faculty members Américo Mendoza-Mori, assistant professor of romance languages; Mariana Reyes Payán, assistant professor of romance languages; León Narváez, professor of romance languages and Latin American studies; Nathan Norris, visiting assistant professor of history; and me. Her participation shows how undergraduate research grows through relationships among students, faculty, staff, community partners, and scholarly organizations. 

The value of her project began with the local relationships that made it possible. Presenting at NCCLA offered another opportunity to share that work, hear other perspectives, and contribute to conversations about Latinidad, migration, and belonging. 

As I reflect on the final year of my appointment as the O.C. and Patricia Boldt Endowed Chair in the Humanities, I see the Boldt family’s generosity as part of a larger network that connects classroom learning, community-engaged research, and public scholarship. This support becomes tangible through mentorship, research time, travel, and opportunities for students to share their work. 

The Svoboda Center for Civic Engagement is an important part of this network. Under Alyssa Melby’s direction, the center supports academic civic engagement (ACE) and fosters connections between courses and community partners. Northfield Public Library’s Outreach Manager Angélica Linder’s community relationships also belong in this story, alongside the knowledge, time, and contributions of community partners themselves. 

Collaborative Undergraduate Research and Inquiry (CURI) and the Digital Scholarship Center at St. Olaf (DiSCO) contribute further opportunities and expertise. Instructional Technologist for Geospatial and Data Services Sara Lynnore’s work with StoryMaps and other digital tools has helped students and faculty make research accessible to public audiences and explore collaborative ways of presenting it. 

The work of Ahmed Sajidan (Saji) Jarjis Rafsan ’27 with the Caribbean Studies Network and its Caribbean Studies Lab offers another example. He helped shape the lab’s development and identified The Caribbean Digital XII conference as a place to bring our work into a wider conversation. Together, we presented the lab’s work at the international gathering in Boston. 

The conference connected our project with scholars working at the intersection of Caribbean studies and digital humanities. For a student involved in developing a research initiative, such exchanges offer a chance to explain methodological choices, learn from other projects, and build relationships beyond St. Olaf. 

These opportunities build on a longer history. St. Olaf’s Latin American Studies program, shaped in large part by Narváez’s longstanding work, has sustained connections with NCCLA and the wider field. Courses such as Mendoza-Mori’s “Imagining Latinidad,” Reyes Payán’s work on Latinx experiences and health care, and my teaching on displacement, activism, and belonging invite students to bring their experiences and questions into academic inquiry. 

Community-engaged scholarship also requires ongoing attention to how research is conducted and shared. Who shapes the questions? How are participants represented? What do community partners gain from the work? Institutional support can help sustain these conversations, but reciprocity depends on the choices researchers make and the relationships they maintain. 

Pérez’s oral-history project and Rafsan’s digital scholarship make these connections visible. When St. Olaf invests in students and in the relationships that sustain their research, local knowledge can reach wider audiences while remaining accountable to the communities from which it grows. Our students are already contributing to those conversations.

title.rendered: Oles in the News: Professor weighs in on whether AI is contributing to the national GDP

content.rendered:
Assistant Professor of Economics Ethan Struby at St. Olaf College was recently featured in Marketplace on the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) investment in the economy.

In the article, the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that “the U.S. economy grew at an annualized rate of 2.2 percent in the second quarter, an upward revision from the previous estimate of 1.5 percent.” 

Struby provided expert insight on how the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure is contributing to gross domestic product (GDP) growth. He explained that companies are building data centers, expanding utility transmission, and constructing on-site power generation to support the growing demand for AI technology. He also noted that many of the chips and other equipment used in this infrastructure are imported, meaning those imports are subtracted from domestic economic growth.

He also offered perspective on the longer-term economic implications of the AI boom. While companies are investing heavily in AI with the expectation that it will increase productivity, he cautioned that its ultimate impact remains uncertain.

“The IT boom in the 1990s didn’t contribute as much to productivity as you might have expected, given how it seemed like it transformed all of our lives,” he says, drawing comparisons to the dot-com bubble.

Read or listen to the original story at Marketplace.

St. Olaf College advisors and career coaches connect students to a menu of more than 5,000 internships, undergraduate research experiences, and other hands-on opportunities at a breadth of organizations ranging from nonprofits to Fortune 500 companies. More than 90 percent of Oles participate in internships, research, and other opportunities to prepare for their future — with robust support from the Piper Center for Vocation and Career. As part of a new series, we’re sharing reflections from Oles on their summer internship and research experiences.

For St. Olaf College students, summer internships offer a chance to take what they’ve learned on the Hill and put it into practice — while discovering new interests, building professional skills, and exploring where their education might lead.

This summer, Oles pursued opportunities across a wide range of fields and locations, gaining hands-on experience in everything from research and business to the arts, health care, and public service. We asked students to share a glimpse into where their internships took them, what they worked on, and what they learned along the way.

“The most impactful part of my experience was getting to chat with other lawyers and members of the legal profession. I had always believed that I had to take the LSAT and go to law school right after St. Olaf, but hearing multiple experiences really reminded me that the law is such a broad field and no one has the same journey.”

— Araba Akyianu ’27, reflecting on her Svoboda Legal Scholars Program in St. Paul, Minnesota

“The most impactful part of this experience was realizing that I genuinely enjoy the process of becoming a physician. Working alongside physicians, pharmacists, residents, and poison specialists also showed me how collaborative medicine truly is. This experience not only strengthened my confidence in pursuing medical school, but also gave me a greater appreciation for academic medicine and lifelong learning.”

— Jeremey Cownover ’27, reflecting on his Rockswold Health Scholars Program in Minneapolis, Minnesota

“The most impactful part of my experience was getting to help sort product donations and connecting with those nonprofits where the product went. Through the product donation process, I was able to see firsthand the impact our product has on people and communities.”

— Julia Grayson ’27, reflecting on her Corporate Social Responsibility Internship with Red Wing Shoe Company in Red Wing, Minnesota

“Taking a very humanistic approach, Hennepin Healthcare physicians and researchers that I shadowed and worked with this summer acted as advocates, defenders, and therapists for each of their patients, seeking to meet needs that transcended the physical. I hope to embody this practice in my future medical career, and this summer experience confirmed for me that medicine is where I belong!”

— Abrianna Nissley ’27, reflecting on her Rockswold Health Scholars Program experience in Minneapolis, Minnesota

“Brevard has multiple orchestras that the students rotate through, but in my first week I got to play with the Brevard Music Center Orchestra (BMCO), which is a mix of faculty and students. I played second harp alongside the harp faculty member, and it was so inspiring to me to watch a professional up close in action. Aside from this, getting to build connections with other harpists from all over the country has been very fulfilling, and they are relationships I hope to keep for a long time!”

— Amalia Ranstrom ’27, reflecting on her experience at Brevard College Orchestral Institute in Brevard, North Carolina
